title: The Eighteenth Vow
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Answer: To deliver beings throughout the ten directions far and wide, Amitābha Buddha made forty-eight great vows. Among them, the eighteenth vow is: "If, when I attain buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere hearts of faith and joy, wish to be born in my land, and even to ten recitations - if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excepted are those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the true Dharma." (The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra)

inline.s: Question: What is the eighteenth vow?
Answer: To deliver beings throughout the ten directions far and wide, Amitābha Buddha made forty-eight great vows. Among them, the eighteenth vow is:

"If, when I attain buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere hearts of faith and joy, wish to be born in my land, and even to ten recitations - if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excepted are those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the true Dharma."
(The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra)

[Five grave offenses] Killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing schism in the Saṅgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha. Because they betray and repay kindness with ingratitude, they are called the five grave offenses.

Question: Does this "even to ten recitations" mean ten recitations in ordinary times, or ten recitations at the moment of death? The Original Vow school holds that "those who recite the Name will certainly be reborn," and it opposes cultivation. Its reasoning is: "The meaning of the eighteenth vow (the Original Vow), the very root of the Pure Land school, is this: as long as one recites the Buddha's name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times ('even to ten recitations'), one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at death ('if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment')." Is this correct?
Answer: The "even to ten recitations" spoken of in the eighteenth vow does not refer to ordinary times,
but to ten recitations at the moment of death
. The reasons are as follows:
1. The eighteenth vow was proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha in The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra.
In this sutra,
the Buddha exhorted:
Though one toils bitterly for a single lifetime
, in the briefest instant one is afterward born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where bliss is boundless."
At the end of the sutra, the Buddha further warned with deep earnestness:
"You should believe and comply,
and cultivate in accordance with the Dharma
If

"even to ten recitations" meant "as long as one recites the Buddha's name ten times in ordinary times, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss," why would the Buddha exhort "
Though one toils bitterly for a single lifetime
"? Why would the Buddha at the end still warn, "
cultivate in accordance with the Dharma

"? Following their distortion of "even to ten recitations," the Original Vow school asserts that "those who recite the Name will certainly be reborn; there is no need to observe precepts, no need to do good, no need to purify one's own mind - even a lifetime of evildoing does not matter," and it teaches the "evil person as the true target" doctrine (see
The Original Vow School Is a Non-Buddhist Sect Masquerading as Buddhism
, an article), and it opposes cultivation. This is utterly wrong.
The Buddha taught
"cultivate in accordance with the Dharma,"
yet they oppose cultivation - this is to stand squarely against the Buddha.

. The Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas' Protection was praised and embraced by the buddhas of the ten directions (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss). Our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha clearly taught in that sutra:

"If there are good men or good women of pure faith who hear the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, with its immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable virtues, and the adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and having heard it, reflect on it for one day and night, or two, three, four, five, six, or seven days and nights,
with unwavering mindfulness
. Such
(these)
good men or good women, at the time of death, will be surrounded before and behind by the Buddha of Immeasurable Life together with his immeasurable host of śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas,
who will come and stand before them,
and with compassion will aid and bless them,

causing their minds to be undisturbed. When their lives have ended, they will follow that assembly of the Buddha and be born in the pure buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life."

Therefore, the requirement for certain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is: unwavering mindfulness. Precisely because one has already attained unwavering mindfulness in ordinary times, one can be assured of accomplishing the ten recitations at the moment of death and is thus certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. If in The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow refers to ten recitations in ordinary times

, then why would our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha still teach "with unwavering mindfulness, ..., be born in that buddha-land"? Why would he again and again enjoin in the sutra, "cultivate as taught," and warn with deep earnestness, "do not give rise to doubt" and "do not act with heedlessness"? Moreover, this teaching
is praised and embraced by the buddhas of the ten directions (which of course includes Amitābha Buddha) - why is that?
(see for details
The Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas' Protection
Therefore, this proves that
the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow is not ten recitations in ordinary times, but ten recitations at the moment of death.

. Master Shandao was a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha. Of Master Shandao, Master Yinguang - himself a manifestation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta - praised: "Master Shandao is an emanation of Amitābha; he possessed great spiritual powers and great wisdom." (From Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
A Letter in Reply to a Layman of Yongjia and His Brothers.) Therefore, the words spoken by Master Shandao are equivalent to those spoken by Amitābha Buddha himself.
Master Shandao taught:
"When illness is grave and death approaches, relatives must not shed tears or weep, nor utter sounds of lamentation and distress that confuse and disturb the mind,
causing loss of right mindfulness
. Instead, all should together recite the Buddha's name in one voice; only after the breath has ceased may they mourn and weep.
The slightest thought of attachment to the world becomes an obstruction, and one cannot be liberated
. It is a great fortune if someone who understands the Pure Land frequently comes to encourage and urge one on. Those who follow this will certainly be reborn there beyond doubt."
see for details
An Annotation on Master Shandao's "Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth"
) In this Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death for Rebirth, Master Shandao continued:

Whether monks, laypeople, or those who have never recited the Buddha's name apply this method, all will be reborn; have no doubt. I have often seen people who in ordinary times recite the Buddha's name and bow in praise, vowing to seek rebirth in the West with great diligence and earnestness
(earnest and sincere)
. Yet when illness comes, they fear death and speak not at all of rebirth and liberation. Only when the breath has gone and life has ended,
and consciousness has fallen into the dark realm
, do they begin ten recitations. That is like shutting the door after the thief has gone - what use is it? The matter of birth and death is grave,
and one must exert one's own effort
A single mistaken thought brings suffering through kalpas
. Who can take your place? Think of this! Think of this! When there is nothing the matter, you should take up this method
with diligence and uphold it
, for this is
the great matter at the time of death

Master Shandao was a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, and his teaching on "right mindfulness at the time of death" proves that the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow means ten recitations at the moment of death. For if the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow meant ten recitations in ordinary times, why would Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, still speak of "right mindfulness at the time of death"? Moreover, throughout his life Master Shandao vigorously advocated upholding The Buddha Speaks of the Amitābha Sutra, and he personally wrote out more than one hundred thousand copies to distribute to his disciples and the faithful, urging them to cultivate as taught: with single-minded focus, the Buddha will surely come to welcome them. If ten recitations in ordinary times sufficed for rebirth, why would Master Shandao have written out more than one hundred thousand copies of The Buddha Speaks of the Amitābha Sutra to distribute to his disciples and the faithful? He need only have written the four words "ten recitations bring rebirth" or "reciting the Name brings certain rebirth."
This proves that the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow is not ten recitations in ordinary times, but ten recitations at the moment of death.

. Master Yongming was a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha; therefore his birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, is observed as Amitābha Buddha's birthday. Of Master Yongming, Master Yinguang - himself a manifestation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta - praised: "Master Yongming is an emanation of Amitābha Buddha. Greatly compassionate and greatly merciful, he opens and transforms sentient beings." (From Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Dharma Talks Given at the World Buddhist Lay Association.) Therefore, the words spoken by Master Yongming are equivalent to those spoken by Amitābha Buddha himself.
Master Yongming taught:
"When walking the path
(that is, walking meditation)
and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha's name and making vows, one should be earnest and sincere,
free of all stray thoughts
, as though facing execution or confined in prison
(bi lao: a prison cell)

, pursued by hateful thieves, pressed by water and fire, single-mindedly seeking rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly realizing non-arising, widely delivering sentient beings, upholding and prospering the Three Jewels, vowing to repay the four kindnesses - with such sincerity, one's efforts will surely not be spent in vain. If one's words and actions do not match
(words and actions do not accord)
, one's power of faith is weak and slight, lacking
the mind of continuous mindfulness
, with repeated interruptions
(the recitation is interrupted by deluded thoughts)
- relying on this indolence, hoping for rebirth at the time of death, one will be veiled by karmic hindrances, and I fear one will hardly meet good friends
(I fear it will be hard to meet a good teacher who can help one accomplish right mindfulness at the time of death)
; wind and fire press upon one, and right mindfulness is not accomplished
(one cannot accomplish right mindfulness at the time of death, and therefore cannot be reborn)
. Why is this?
The present is the cause; the time of death is the effect
. The cause must be real, and then the effect will not be empty. If one wishes
to accomplish the ten recitations at the time of death
, one should prepare the ford and bridge in advance, gather merit, and dedicate it to that time
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, never deficient in mindfulness
(so that mindfulness continues without interruption)
, and then there is nothing to worry about."
(From The Compendium of Myriad Good Practices Returning to the One)

[Words and actions do not match] Words and actions do not accord. One says aloud that one has true faith and sincere vows, yet in actual conduct one's faith is not true and one's vow is not sincere: one fears hardship and fears suffering, one is lazy and indolent. Hence Master Yongming's next line is:
"one's power of faith is weak and slight."
And he rebuked them, saying:
"relying on this indolence."
Those who recite the Buddha's name should keep firmly in mind the Buddha's earnest teaching in the Immeasurable Life Sutra:
Though one toils bitterly for a single lifetime
, in the briefest instant one is afterward born in the Land of Immeasurable Life,
where bliss is boundless
[Accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death] Accomplishing the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death.
[Prepare the ford and bridge in advance] "Ford and bridge" means a crossing and a bridge. "Preparing the ford and bridge in advance" means making preparations beforehand.
Master Yongming was a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, and his teaching on "accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death"
proves that the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow is not ten recitations in ordinary times, but ten recitations at the moment of death
. For if the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow meant ten recitations in ordinary times, why would Master Yongming, a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, still speak of "
accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death

Only the final decision at the time of death is the true decision. At the moment of death it is like a person arriving at an airport: in ordinary times he says he wants to go here or there, but where he actually ends up depends entirely on which plane he finally boards (even if he is confused, in the end it is he himself who walks aboard). That is the final vow, the final decision. Therefore,
accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death is utterly crucial
Conclusion one: From this we know that the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow
means ten recitations at the moment of death

Question: Does "ten recitations at the time of death bring rebirth" mean that as long as one recites the Buddha's name ten times at the time of death, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: These ten recitations are
utterly sincere
ten recitations (
"with sincere hearts of faith and joy"
Utterly sincere means the mind is pure and undefiled.
Therefore the utterly sincere ten recitations
are recitations of the Buddha's name, ten recitations in continuous mindfulness (ten recitations of the Buddha's name unmixed with deluded thoughts).
"Ten recitations at the time of death bring rebirth," specifically means: ten continuous recitations at the time of death ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Therefore, the ten continuous recitations at the time of death (ten recitations of the Buddha's name unmixed with deluded thoughts) - these are what the eighteenth vow calls
"with sincere hearts of faith and joy, wishing to be born in my land, even to ten recitations"
the ten recitations.
Utterly sincere means pure and undefiled

. If at this crucial moment one still mixes other thoughts into the recitation, then it cannot be called "sincere hearts of faith and joy, wishing to be born in my land" - how could one then resonate and connect with Amitābha Buddha? Master Yinguang said:

"The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings' faith and vows are complete and they sincerely move the Buddha, the Buddha responds, just as when the water is clear the moon appears. But if the mind is not pure, not sincere, in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and turned away from the Buddha, then it is like turbid and moving water: though the moon never fails to shine upon it, it cannot clearly reflect its image."
(Master Yinguang's Collected Writings: Preface to A Beginner's Guide to Pure Karma)
This is what Master Shandao called "
continuity brings rebirth
," and what Master Yongming called "
accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death

" (before speaking of "accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death," Master Yongming had already spoken of "free of all stray thoughts" and "the mind of continuous mindfulness" - see the passage quoted above). It is also what Master Yinguang called "
apart from this thought, absolutely no other thought
." Master Yinguang said:
"In the Contemplation Sutra, when those who have committed the five grave offenses and the ten evils are about to die, the marks of hell appear. If there is a good teacher
(original note: whether monk or lay, man or woman, whoever can teach such a person to recite the Buddha's name is called a good teacher.)

who teaches them to recite the Buddha's name, whether for only ten recitations or fewer than ten, and they die straightaway, they too may rely on the Buddha's compassionate power and be reborn with their karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, are so fierce and urgent that the difference is as vast as heaven and an abyss; hence they attain rebirth. Because they are pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, as soon as they hear the Buddha's name they recite it with their whole spirit.
apart from this thought, absolutely no other thought
Though this is not personally realizing single-minded focus, their minds nonetheless are utterly free of other thoughts.
(From the Third Collection of Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Volume Two
A Letter in Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru.) The Two Gates of Doubt-Dispelling Vow and Practice for Rebirth in the Pure Land says:
"Though one was evil and rebellious,
with ten sincere recitations
one is born in that land."
Therefore,
in order to ensure the continuity of the ten recitations at the time of death,
Master Shandao earnestly admonished:
Precisely because reciting the Name is easy
(it is precisely because holding the Name in recitation is easier to accomplish than visualization-recitation)
continuity brings rebirth
If one can
continue mindfulness without interruption

, making this one's aim for the whole of one's life, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. ...... May all people reflect well on this: while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must discipline the mind and restrain oneself, never neglecting this day or night."
For the details of Master Shandao's teaching on "continuity brings rebirth," see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
, an article.
[Continuity brings rebirth]
"Continuity brings rebirth" means:
at the time of death, the thought of reciting the Buddha's name continues without interruption
(not interrupted by deluded thoughts)
, and one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The word "continuity" here means the thought of reciting the Buddha's name follows thought upon thought with no deluded thoughts interposed (if deluded thoughts intrude, it is not continuity). One must never misunderstand the word "continuity" here as the sound of recitation continuing on the lips while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind. As the saying goes, an error by a hair's breadth leads astray by a thousand miles. [Continue mindfulness without interruption, making this one's aim for the whole of one's life] Because at the time of death the continuity of the thought of reciting the Buddha's name brings rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one should practice in this way for one's whole life,
causing the thought of reciting the Buddha's name to continue and, through accumulated habit, to become one's nature

. In this way one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss - ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. [Through accumulated habit, to become one's nature] means that by constantly repeated practice, the continuity of the thought of reciting the Buddha's name becomes second nature.

[Discipline the mind and restrain oneself] To spur oneself on and to restrain oneself. The four words "discipline the mind and restrain oneself" are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles. "Restrain oneself" means to control oneself.
[Never neglecting day or night] Day and night, never cease the continuity of mindfulness.
In order to ensure the continuity of the ten recitations at the time of death,
Master Yongming taught:
"When walking the path
(that is, walking meditation)
and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha's name and making vows, one should be earnest and sincere,
free of all stray thoughts
, as though facing execution or confined in prison
(bi lao: a prison cell)

, pursued by hateful thieves, pressed by water and fire, single-mindedly seeking rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly realizing non-arising, widely delivering sentient beings, upholding and prospering the Three Jewels, vowing to repay the four kindnesses - with such sincerity, one's efforts will surely not be spent in vain. If one's words and actions do not match, one's power of faith is weak and slight, lacking
the mind of continuous mindfulness
, while having the intention of repeated interruptions
(the recitation is interrupted by deluded thoughts)
- relying on this indolence, hoping for rebirth at the time of death, one will be veiled by karmic hindrances, and I fear one will hardly meet good friends
(I fear it will be hard to meet a good teacher who can give rise to right mindfulness at the time of death for such a person)
; wind and fire press upon one, and right mindfulness is not accomplished. Why is this?
The present is the cause; the time of death is the effect
. The cause must be real, and then the effect will not be empty. If one wishes
to accomplish the ten recitations at the time of death
, one should prepare the ford and bridge in advance, gather merit, and dedicate it to that time
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, never deficient in mindfulness
(so that mindfulness continues without interruption)
, and then there is nothing to worry about."
(From The Compendium of Myriad Good Practices Returning to the One)
Please note that Master Yongming said: if

"one lacks the mind of continuous mindfulness and has the intention of repeated interruptions," then rebirth is difficult. Therefore, what Master Yongming called "accomplishing the ten recitations at the time of death" means accomplishing the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death. "Dedicate it to that time" means dedicating it to the moment of death; "never deficient in mindfulness" means mindfulness continues without interruption. So "dedicate it to that time, never deficient in mindfulness" means dedicating to the moment of death a continuity of mindfulness. In this way, "there is nothing to worry about" (that is, one can be assured of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss).
On this point, Master Daochuo also taught in The Collection of the Land of Peace and Joy:
At the time of death for all sentient beings
, the knife-like wind dismembers the body, the suffering of death presses in, and great terror arises. Therefore, if one meets a good teacher, arouses great courage and vigor,
and recites ten times with mind following mind in continuity
, this is a surpassing good root,
and one attains rebirth
Please note that Master Daochuo teaches here: at the time of death for all sentient beings, ten recitations with mind following mind in continuity bring rebirth. In other words:
ten recitations at the time of death - continuity brings rebirth.

[The knife-like wind] When a person is dying, they endure the suffering of death and the four elements separate. Among these, the wind that dismembers the joints like a knife is called the "knife-like wind." The Sutra of the Mindfulness of the True Dharma says: "When one sees the end of life, the knife-like winds all stir, and skin, flesh, sinews and bones, fat, marrow, essence and blood are all cut apart." The Sutra of the Five Kings says: "When about to die, the knife-like wind dismembers the body, and there is no place that does not hurt."
Therefore, as to the meaning of the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo clearly taught in The Collection of the Land of Peace and Joy:
"If there are sentient beings who, though they have done evil for a whole lifetime,
at the time of death recite ten times in continuity
and call my name,
if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Here Master Daochuo gives a precise exposition of the meaning of "even to ten recitations" in the eighteenth vow:
At the time of death, ten recitations in continuity, calling my name.
Therefore, the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow means ten recitations at the time of death, and moreover ten recitations in continuity.
Conclusion two: From this we know that the "even to ten recitations" of the eighteenth vow
is
ten recitations at the time of death with mindfulness continuing without interruption
Concerning

the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death, Master Daochuo has another very important passage in The Collection of the Land of Peace and Joy, which is transcribed and annotated as follows:

[Question: The Great Sutra of Immeasurable Life says: 'The sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere hearts of faith and joy, wishing to be born in my land, even to ten recitations - if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.' Nowadays there are people in the world who, hearing this sacred teaching, pay no attention to it at all throughout their present lives. They intend to practice recitation only when death approaches. What is to be said of this?]

Question: The Immeasurable Life Sutra says: 'The sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere hearts of faith and joy, wishing to be born in my land, even to ten recitations - if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.' Some people today, hearing this sacred teaching, show it by paying no attention at all. They plan to accomplish the continuity of ten recitations only when death approaches. What do you think of this plan?
[Answer: This matter is of a different kind. Why? The sutra says '
ten recitations in continuity

,' which seems not difficult. Yet all ordinary beings have minds like wild horses and consciousness more restless than monkeys, galloping through the six dusts - when have they ever stopped to rest? Each must arouse a faithful mind and discipline their own thoughts in advance,
so that through accumulated habit it becomes their nature

, and their good roots become firm. As the Buddha told the king: 'When a person accumulates good conduct, at death no evil thought arises; just as a tree that has already leaned will surely fall in that direction.' If the knife-like wind arrives and a hundred sufferings crowd upon the body, and if the habit was not established beforehand, how can one possibly hold the thought in mind
(that is, manage to bring it to mind)

Answer: Such a plan is like digging a well when one is already thirsty. Digging a well when thirsty and preparing the ford and bridge in advance are two quite different things (this matter is of a different kind). Why? The sutra says 'ten recitations in continuity,' which appears not difficult (and so many people assume they will be able to do it at the time of death). Yet all ordinary beings have minds like wild horses and consciousness more restless than monkeys, galloping through the six dusts (the dusts of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects) - when have they ever stopped? Each person must arouse a mind of faith, and beforehand train themselves in single-minded focus and the continuity of ten recitations, so that through accumulated habit it becomes their nature (through constant practice, making single-minded focus and the continuity of ten recitations second nature), and only then will their good roots be firm at the time of death. As the Buddha told the king: 'If people continually accumulate good conduct in ordinary times, then at the time of death no evil thought arises; just as when a tree falls, it must fall in the direction in which it already leaned.' If the knife-like wind of death arrives and a hundred sufferings press in, and one has never beforehand made the continuity of ten recitations a habit, then at the time of death, relying merely on the wish to achieve 'ten recitations in continuity,' how could one possibly succeed?

[Consciousness more restless than monkeys] The six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) are even more frantic than a monkey leaping and bounding about. [Through accumulated habit it becomes their nature] Through repeated practice, making it second nature.

[Each should join with three or five like-minded friends and beforehand make a firm agreement: at the time of death, taking turns to rouse and instruct one another, recite the name of Amitābha and vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Joy, voice following voice in succession, so as to accomplish the ten recitations. It is like a wax seal pressed into clay: the seal is destroyed but the pattern is formed. When this life is cut off, that is the moment of birth in the Land of Peace and Joy. Once one enters the company of those assured of enlightenment, what is there left to worry about? Each should weigh this great benefit - why not train oneself in mindfulness beforehand?]

Therefore, it is best for everyone to invite three or five like-minded friends and agree beforehand: at the time of death, taking turns to rouse and instruct the dying person, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha for them, encourage them to firmly resolve to be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, voice following voice in succession, so as to accomplish the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death. It is like
pressing a wax seal into clay: though the seal is destroyed, the pattern has already been formed;

so the moment the breath stops is the moment of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once one arrives in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one immediately enters the company of those assured of enlightenment - at that point, what is there left to worry about? Everyone should surely reflect on this tremendous benefit: why not train well in the continuity of ten recitations beforehand?
[In succession] One after another. [The wax seal pressed on clay:
the seal
is destroyed
and the pattern (
the decorative motif

) is formed] A wax seal carved with a decorative motif is pressed onto a clay mold. When the clay mold is heated and dried, the wax seal melts, and the decorative motif pressed into the clay mold is formed. The clay mold is a mold used for casting metal vessels.
The Nirvāṇa Sutra says:
"It is like a wax seal pressed on clay: the seal and the clay meet, the seal perishes and the pattern is formed."

Here "the seal is destroyed and the pattern is formed" is a metaphor for our using this physical body to cultivate: having accomplished the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death, when the breath stops, though the physical body dies (the seal is destroyed), the great matter of rebirth is accomplished at the same time (the pattern is formed) - "when this life is cut off, that is the moment of birth in the Land of Peace and Joy." [The company of those assured of enlightenment] One of the three groups. [The three groups] The three groups are the three categories of sentient beings: the group assured of enlightenment, the group of wrong certainty, and the group of uncertainty. The group assured of enlightenment refers to those who will certainly realize enlightenment; the group of wrong certainty refers to those who can never realize enlightenment; the group of uncertainty refers to those between the two who may or may not realize enlightenment. [Why not train oneself in mindfulness beforehand?] Why not train well in the continuity of ten recitations beforehand? This is what Master Yongming called "preparing the ford and bridge in advance" in the passage above.
In The Collection of the Land of Peace and Joy, Master Daochuo has two more very important passages on rebirth through reciting the Buddha's name:
[Even if one has done evil for a whole lifetime,
if only one can focus the mind single-mindedly
, and can constantly recite the Buddha's name, then all hindrances will naturally dissolve and one will certainly attain rebirth.]
This passage means: even if one has done evil for a whole lifetime,
if only, after repenting and reforming,
one can
focus the mind single-mindedly
(with pure mindfulness continuing), and constantly recite the Buddha's name, then all hindrances will naturally dissolve and one will certainly attain rebirth.

Please note: "Even if one has done evil for a whole lifetime" describes the situation before repentance and reform; "if only one can focus the mind single-mindedly and constantly recite the Buddha's name" describes the situation after repentance and reform. For if one has not truly repented and reformed, how could one possibly focus the mind single-mindedly?

[From the utmost, a whole lifetime, down to ten recitations, all without exception attain rebirth. Once one arrives in that land, one immediately enters the company of those assured of enlightenment; this is equal in merit to ten thousand kalpas of cultivating the path here.]

From the utmost, a whole lifetime of continuous mindfulness, down to the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death - all without exception attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once one arrives in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one immediately enters the company of those assured of enlightenment; this is equal in effect to ten thousand kalpas of cultivating the path in the ordinary teachings!

[From the utmost, a whole lifetime, down to ten recitations] Viewed in the context of the whole Collection of the Land of Peace and Joy, the meaning is: from the utmost, a whole lifetime of continuous mindfulness, down to the continuity of ten recitations at the time of death. The ancients prized concision in writing, so in understanding this one must connect the preceding and following passages; never take the words at face value or quote out of context.

We read sutras and the treatises and teachings of the patriarchs and great masters in order to seek the truth. Therefore, one should act with a true heart: whatever a thing is, that is what it is. Never, for the sake of one's own selfish ends, play the trick of quoting out of context - for example, distorting "from the utmost, a whole lifetime, down to ten recitations, all without exception attain rebirth" into: "Master Daochuo says that as long as one recites the Buddha's name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times ('down to ten recitations'), one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at death ('all without exception attain rebirth'). Therefore, reciting the Name brings certain rebirth." The fact is: in the line preceding "from the utmost, a whole lifetime, down to ten recitations, all without exception attain rebirth," Master Daochuo had already stated with complete clarity "
if only one can focus the mind single-mindedly

." So, reading the two lines together, "down to ten recitations" means ten recitations at the time of death with the mind focused single-mindedly (pure mindfulness continuing), not ten recitations with a scattered mind in ordinary times. To quote out of context in this way not only misleads others but also harms oneself.
